name: Bitter melon (Momordica charantia)
short: Review: low-blood-sugar coma and convulsions reported in children. Case reports: severe liver injury, kidney inflammation, pancreatitis with pazopanib. 12-week diabetes trial: no serious events.
text: A 2003 review lists reported adverse effects of bitter melon including hypoglycaemic (low blood sugar) coma and convulsions in children, a favism-like syndrome and headaches, along with reduced fertility in mice and raised liver enzymes in animals; it says bitter melon may have additive effects with other glucose-lowering agents and that the data were not sufficient to recommend its use without careful supervision and monitoring. Case reports describe liver injury: a 61-year-old man with previously treated hepatitis C who drank a bitter melon herbal tea in large quantities had liver enzymes in the thousands, with causality rated highly probable, and had a positive outcome; a 38-year-old man who reported occasional alcohol use and had taken several herbal remedies, including bitter melon, for two to three weeks had herb-induced liver injury supported by liver biopsy and improved after stopping them. Single case reports also describe acute interstitial nephritis (kidney inflammation) in a 60-year-old woman after 7 months of a pure bitter melon extract, with kidney function almost back to baseline 3 months after stopping it and starting steroid treatment, and acute pancreatitis in a 65-year-old man on the cancer medicine pazopanib after 4 days of bitter melon extract, which the authors thought might reflect an interaction and rated as a probable association, while noting that pancreatitis has also been reported with pazopanib itself. Two letters, without abstracts, are titled as reports of vomiting blood from bitter melon extract-induced stomach ulcers and of atrial fibrillation due to bitter melon. In contrast, a 12-week randomised placebo-controlled trial of bitter melon extract as an add-on treatment in people with type 2 diabetes (90 included in the analysis of glucose-lowering efficacy; the abstract does not give the number assessed for safety) reported no serious adverse events during the treatment period. In pregnant rats, a dry extract of bitter melon leaves (not the fruit) reduced food intake and weight gain, which the authors called low maternal toxicity, without marked effects on reproductive outcomes or on skeletal malformations in the offspring.
